title: IonQ to acquire Elisity for $1.3 billion to bolster quantum security
source_used: IonQ press release (ionq.com, 12 Oct 2026) and The Quantum Insider report citing The Wall Street Journal (12 Oct 2026); SC Media page blocked
key_facts: IonQ (NYSE: IONQ) announced on 12 Oct 2026 a definitive agreement to acquire Elisity, Inc., a Zero Trust security company, in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.
The price includes up to $150 million of earnout tied to how the Elisity business performs.
Closing is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026 and needs customary conditions including regulatory approval.

Elisity, founded in 2019, sells software meant to stop attackers and ransomware spreading inside an organisation's network; the WSJ (via The Quantum Insider) says its customers include health care companies and hospitals; IonQ cites more than 100 customer deployments.

IonQ chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi said "Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted" and told the WSJ that US companies and the federal government must prepare for the point when quantum computers can defeat widely used public-key cryptography.
IonQ shares issued will be priced between $33.07 and $49.61 each; IonQ closed Friday 9 Oct 2026 at $39.89 (WSJ via The Quantum Insider).

The deal follows IonQ's $1.8 billion purchase of chipmaker SkyWater Technology, likely its largest acquisition to date (WSJ via The Quantum Insider); IonQ announced completion of that deal on 31 Jul 2026.
Elisity CEO James Winebrenner is expected to stay on after closing.
quote_evidence: Under the terms of the agreement, IonQ will acquire Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in earnout opportunity subject to performance of the Elisity business.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approval.
Its major customers include health care companies and hospitals, according to the WSJ.
why_it_matters_hint: A quantum computing company is buying network-security software, arguing customers need both ordinary cyber defence and preparation for the day quantum computers can break today's encryption.
